pages.title: Delivered trips
pages.content:
Delivered.

Forty-one programmes since 2012, from a 38-guest sales leaders’ trek to a 120-guest reward trip to Cape Town. Each one is listed here with its headcount, length and per-guest price.

The four most recent cases sit on the home page; this page carries the full wall.

pages.title: Programmes
pages.content:
Programmes.

Four programme types for groups of 20 to 120 guests: the short-haul reward trip, the long-haul reward trip, the sales-team retreat and the kick-off summit.

Prices start at €980 per guest for a two-night retreat and €1,850 per guest for a three-night short-haul trip. One tour director per 30 guests is always included.

pages.title: How we plan
pages.content:
Five stages.

A programme runs from the budget and the reward rule in week one to the debrief ten working days after the return flight.

Ideal lead time is six to twelve months; the minimum is ten weeks.

pages.title: Destinations
pages.content:
Six places.

Lisbon and Sintra, the Dolomites, Cape Town and the winelands, Copenhagen, Seville and the Andalusian coast, and the south coast of Iceland: twenty-three destinations visited so far, six of them described here.

Every destination is costed three ways before a team chooses.

pages.title: About
pages.content:
Since 2012.

Hobi Journeys was founded in 2012 by Maren Holt and Daniel Okoro in Port Arden after planning the sales trip of a former employer. The name comes from turning the everyday into a day out.

Our first programme took 38 guests to Lisbon. Today we run groups of 20 to 120 guests with our own tour-director team.

pages.title: Brief us
pages.content:
Brief us.

Tell us the team size, the month you would like to travel, a budget per guest and who qualifies. We reply within two working days and propose three costed destinations in three weeks.

posts.title: Why we still hand out boarding passes
posts.excerpt: A physical document at the check-in desk creates a tangible hand-over from the working year to the journey ahead.
posts.content:
Every programme begins at a desk. A tour director stands behind it with a folder, a printed boarding pass for each guest and a day sheet folded in thirds. It is the oldest ritual in group travel and we have not found a reason to replace it.

A printed pass does something a phone cannot: it is handed over. For the length of that exchange the guest is looked at, greeted by name and told the first three things that will happen. The working year ends there, at a desk, with a person.

It also keeps the desk honest. A tour director who has handed out ninety-six passes knows, before the coach doors open, exactly who is present and who is not. That count, repeated at every transfer, is most of the job.

posts.title: Writing a reward rule your team believes
posts.excerpt: How clear qualification criteria and honest milestone tracking keep a sales team motivated across four quarters.
posts.content:
A reward trip is only as motivating as the rule that earns it. Teams read the rule in the first week of the year and test it against what they know about their own pipeline. If it feels arbitrary, they stop believing in the trip.

The rules that work are short, measurable and visible. One number, one date and a place where everyone can see where they stand at the end of each quarter. We ask clients to write the rule before we cost the first destination.

Where a rule has changed mid-year the trip has usually suffered. If the target must move, say so early, say why and keep the destination fixed. The team is travelling towards a place, not a spreadsheet.

posts.title: The day after the return flight
posts.excerpt: Closing the loop with itemised budget reconciliation, supplier settlement and a team debrief within ten working days.
posts.content:
The programme is not finished when the group lands. The day after the return flight our planner reopens the budget and compares it, line by line, with what was spent on the trip.

Within ten working days the client receives an itemised reconciliation, a list of supplier settlements and a short debrief from the tour directors: what worked, what to change and what the guests said at the last dinner.

The debrief is the first page of the next brief. Most of our repeat programmes begin with it.
